title: Trump’s Bumbling, Racist Anti-China Protectionism Extends To Data Centers
text:
Overhype

The Trump administration’s anti-Chinese protectionism is routinely a disastrous, xenophobic mess that mostly just injects chaos, cronyism, and higher prices into U.S. tech markets under the pretense of protecting privacy and national security. All propped up by bumbling Democrats and a corporate press incapable of highlighting that the emperor is buck-ass naked.

Four years of histrionics about China’s connection to TikTok, for example, simply resulted in the administration with Democrat help) hijacking the platform and giving it to his billionaire buddies, who’ll then do all the same things lawmakers worried about China doing (propaganda, privacy abuses).

There was also a massive, decade-long hysterical freak-out about Huawei gear in U.S. telecom networks, which resulted in the government engaging in a massive “rip and replace” campaign that Congress simply forgot to finish funding or following up on, resulting in higher prices for consumers and telecoms alike.

More recently there was the Trump FCC’s efforts to try and ban Chinese drones based on completely baseless security fear mongering, which overseas companies have found it trivial to bypass because the administration has mostly lobotomized our regulators. The result has been higher consumer prices, lots of market chaos, furious hobbyists, and shittier product availability.

The Trump administration is utterly incompetent, historically corrupt, and completely incapable of adopting protectionism at this scale even if it was a good idea (it’s not). Yet that’s not really been well reflected in most journalism covering the steady extension of this bumbling protectionism into Chinese routers, robots, vacuums, lawnmowers, and cheap inverters (necessary to manage climate change mitigation).

Now the Trump administration is pretending it’s going to eliminate the entirety of Chinese hardware — including transceivers — from domestic U.S. data centers. Again there’s zero real indication the Trump administration is capable of any of this, but that’s not really reflected in coverage by Reuters. Though they do bother to mention this will likely result in higher prices for everybody:

“A ban could also raise costs ‌for American cloud ⁠firms such as Amazon Web Services, as it may force them to transition to other producers such as U.S.-based Coherent and Lumentum.”

This bumbling protectionism highlights the bizarre incoherence of the Trump administration. The underlying corruption has the administration fixated on gutting, defunding, and destaffing regulators now managed by a rotating crop of unqualified sycophants. But they then like to pretend they can then place these elaborate policy proposals on the back of whatever’s left, and expect it all to just work.

They despise and hate competent governance and regulatory autonomy, do everything in their power to dismantle it, then pretend the resulting pile of garbage remains load-bearing for real policy.

At the same time, the administration professes to be shoring up U.S. cybersecurity defenses while simultaneously dismantling domestic cybersecurity preparedness. It’s an incoherent mess, and more often than not Trump cybersecurity policy is indistinguishable from a foreign attack.

What Trumpism mostly wants is a tribute system wherein they erect new barriers to market entry, then receive assorted tribute by companies that want to still operate in the country. They also want to redirect more business to the administration’s friends, donors, and family (like the Trump sons’ drone companies). Time and time again, national security and privacy are mostly just used for scare-mongering purposes.

Worse, Democrats often help them and frequently aren’t much better. See for example this effort by Dem lawmakers in Michigan to ban Chinese EVs from even visiting the state under the pretense of protecting U.S. consumer privacy. Or their massive policy own-goal on supporting a ban of TikTok during an election season where authoritarianism was on the line, and the youth vote mattered more than ever.

Ideally, I’d maintain that the best approach is to let Chinese gear (EVs, robots, AI, vacuums, drones) compete in the U.S. market, but shore up your labor, privacy, environmental, and consumer protection regulators to ensure a truly level playing field. Domestic U.S. corporate giants don’t like that because it means more competition and oversight, so instead we get this clumsy, corrupt absurdism.

Even if anti-Chinese protectionism was a good idea (it’s not), this administration is too corrupt, erratic, and incompetent to accomplish it. Yet when you’re reading tech press coverage of Trump’s latest protectionist push, I’d like you to notice how that’s uniformly either downplayed or ignored entirely.

Filed Under: ai, china, chinese, data centers, drones, hardware, protectionism

the bizarre incoherence of the Trump administration

That’s what happens when you put unrepentant bigots and people without any real knowledge/expertise in a given field enough power: They use it so stupidly and with so little foresight into the consequences of using that power that it seems incoherent to everyone else, even though it makes perfect sense to the people using said power. It’s like how Trump thinks spreading the MMR vaccine into multiple shots is a good idea⁠—sure, it sounds logical on its face, but looking a millimeter beyond the surface reveals a bunch of problems with the idea. (One of those problems is how spacing out those vaccinations puts a strain on parents, who now how to worry about the stress of multiple separate trips to the doctor for their child instead of one.) Sensible thinking isn’t a hallmark of these idiots; if anything, I’m surprised things aren’t worse due to their idiocy. Then again, there are two years left in his term…

For that executive order to be implemented it would take a drug company to develop, test, and get approval for the vaccines.  I don’t think any can do it before he’s out of office.

I also doubt any major drug companies are willing to invest the money for the project because it would need almost immediate payback to be profitable since the policy will likely be gone once Trump is out of office.

Monovalent vaccines for do exist.  Or did.  I don’t know if anyone makes them anymore.  The Ars Technica article was inaccurate, or at best misleading.

I was just reading in a reliable source about how Andrew Wakefield was pushing for a return to monovalent vaccines almost thirty years ago, when he first started attacking MMR.  Yes, that Wakefield.  Ex-doctor Wakefield, the father of the modern anti-vaxxer movement.  And he somehow… knows Trump.

Due to EO #14420, I’m now learning details of a story that I only absorbed bits and pieces of over the past three decades—and that I partly forgot.  Like many reasonable people, I tuned out a lot of the MMR drama after Wakefield was exposed as a fraud (note for those who are unaware: it was not an honest scientific mistake!).  I’m now shocked at how much I don’t know—not about vaccines, but about anti-vaxxers.

Given that this subject is OT here, I should save more for the next thread about anti-vaxxers—but for this:  §4 of the EO is not being properly reported, and it is potentially the most dangerous part.

I know monovalent vaccines exist but I don’t think there is a company currently manufacturing it for mmr diseases because the trivalent vaccine has been safe and effective for so long.

I’m almost sure it would take a significant investment in new production to manufacture it at scale and I don’t think drug companies will waste their money on it.

The courts have been throwing out actions by vaccine nut jobs for decades so I don’t think much will change.  Maybe the administration will get counter sued for being arbitrary and capricious… more…

Sometimes I’m overly optimistic though.  There are cranks and nut jobs through the government and they always find a way to disappoint and leave me incredulous.

Ah, I was speaking to “develop, test, and get approval”.  New production at scale would indeed be ridiculous.  (An aside, not for you—when discussing this, it’s important to emphasize for anyone who doesn’t know:  There was never any scientific evidence whatsoever linking MMR to autism.  None.  Zero.  It is not a matter of conflicting or questionable scientific evidence.  Not an 0.0001% chance it could be true.  The MMR-autism link was financially-motivated fraud, intentionally faked by Andrew Wakefield to manufacture evidence for a lawsuit against pharmaceutical companies and in hope of selling quack pseudomedical tests.  It was the single worst scientific fraud in the history of modern medicine.  It’s now U.S. Federal policy.)

The courts have been throwing out actions by vaccine nut jobs for decades so I don’t think much will change. Maybe the administration will get counter sued for being arbitrary and capricious… more…

The courts were more or less protecting Internet free speech, voting rights, and basic abortion rights for decades before… uh… Has Trump gotten us any anti-vaxxer judges yet?  Does anyone even know?  Who even asks about that at a judicial confirmation hearing?  (By the way, with RFK Jr. as U.S. Secretary of Health, do we need to start Borking judicial nominees on their opinion of the germ theory of disease, too?)

Please note that Executive Order 14420 §4 is couched in terms of “parental authority” and “religious freedom”, inter alia.  Both of those terms are fetish objects for the Christian Nationalist Revolutionary Tribunal that currently occupies the U.S. Supreme Court’s building, and likely for many other Trump-appointed judges in the circuit and district courts.

A partial self-correction—what I said was not the whole story:

Andrew Wakefield filed for some monovalent measles vaccine patents in the 1990s.  I don’t yet know details.  I don’t know what his angle was, other than money.  Britain had been using a monovalent measles vaccine just a few years before.  (The U.S. has not since the early 1970s.)

If I were an investigative journalist, I’d now start digging to see if any of Trump’s cronies has any patent rights on a new monovalent vaccine for M, M, and/or R.  I don’t assume so; as I myself only recently learned from an anonymous Techdirt comment, Trump has been pushing this line since not later than 2007.  But I’d look into it.

It would be nice to see all this untangled by a vaccine expert, which I am not.

Wakefield has flooded the zone with so much shit, interpreting it is like trying to keep up with a Gish gallop.  It is why I’ve mostly ignored him in all the years since it was incontrovertibly proved that he faked the evidence linking MMR to autism, and he had undisclosed financial motives for scaring people away from MMR.

Daily reminder to the public that there is no need to prove that MMR does not cause autism.  There is exactly as much evidence that it does cause autism as that MMR causes full-body spontaneous combustion:  Zero.  MMR-autism is not even a fringe theory:  It is a Big Lie.

That’s a really good point: I suspect we’ll see a fair amount of malicious compliance as drug companies count on Trump to be gone in a maximum of 2.5 years.  There will be unavoidable delays and inventory control problems and testing issues and so on, as everyone tries to run out the clock with minimum impact on budgets and public health.

But an enormous amount of effort that could be put into constructive projects will be wasted on this nonsense.

Coherent and Lumentum don’t produce logical chips (like CPUs and GPUs) but network components and captors.
Intel still relies on TSMC and Samsung for its graphics cards and I/O devices.
AMD and Nvidia are fabless companies, they design theirs own chips but all are built by TSMC.
US don’t produce any RAM.
So yes, China, Taiwan and Korea produces +90% of datacenters components (and certainly 99% of AI datacenters).

(and certainly 99% of AI datacenters).

On second thought, this particular Trump policy is accidentally a good idea.  Stopped clock, twice a day, etc.

Micron produces RAM, but I don’t know if it does at its domestic facilities.

My understanding (see below) is they have moved away from consumer RAM as AI RAM is a different solution affecting the process chain

AI RAM is expensive so there is dramatically more profit in data center support

This is below: yet, I could find no verification on their web site

May we please stop calling this “protectionism”?  Trump’s policy is even less protective than a “protection” racket:  It is setting fire to your own store and then kneecapping yourself, because—um, because.

Trade protectionism needs to protect someone’s economic interests against market competition.  This is mindless trade destructionism.

Trump’s trade policy is “protectionist” only in the same sense that RFK Jr. protects Americans’ health, the Trumpified EPA protects the environment, Trump’s voting rights policy protects election integrity, Trump protects freedom of speech, Trump protects religious freedom, TRAP laws and abortion bans protect life, Trump protects American Greatness, etc., etc., ad Magnam nauseam.

“Domestic U.S. corporate giants don’t like that because it means more competition and oversight, so instead we get this clumsy, corrupt absurdism.”

One of best and easiest things we could do — in the interest of US national security — would be shut down Flock entirely and immediately.

Because all that beautiful data is being harvested by any intelligence agency worth of the name and they’re not just doing spot searches on it to stalk ex-girlfriends and other abusive things.  No, they’re storing all of it (because they can) and they’re doing serious analysis (because they can) in order to extract as much actionable intelligence as possible from it.  And the best part — from their point of view — is that they didn’t have to design it, build it, run it, or pay for it.  Flock did that for them, for free.  All they’ve had to do is grab the data, and I have zero doubt that they’ve been doing that since the beginning.

(Surely nobody can believe that Flock put any serious time, effort, or money into security.  And even if they did: they’re no match for the Chinese, or the Russians, or pretty much anybody else.)

It would not surprise me at all to find out that — for example — the Chinese have invested in Flock (through shell companies) and/or lobbied for Flock (through shell organizations) because these would be cheap investments with an enormous payoff.  But this administration is far, far too stupid to consider this or to investigate it or to do something about it — and even if they tried, whatever they did would be easily derailed by a $10M Flock contribution to Trump.

The Trump regime executes Americans in the street, but they want us to believe the enemy is across an ocean.

It’s not any more “racist” to be against the CCP than it is to be against Russia, you utter moron.

This is why the word means nothing when you use it.

It’s not any more “racist” to be against the CCP than it is to be against Russia

It is when the only reason people are against the CCP comes down to racism against East Asian people. Russia⁠—which is a significant part of Asia, mind you!⁠—is just as much of a authoritarian capitalist hellscape as China, but Trump is more than happy to give Putin a pass on basically anything because Putin is a white guy. A number of right-wing grifters media personalities were also more than happy to ignore Russia’s crimes until Viktor Orban got ousted from power and all that money he was paying those people dried up.

OP considers it woke that Trump doesn’t consider Slavs subhuman.

It’s not any more “racist” to be against the CCP than it is to be against Russia, you utter moron.

How does ruining the U.S. economy defeat the CCP?

China has a large, diversified economy with well-developed primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors, and numerous international trading partners.  It’s not as dependent on exports to the U.S. as it was some decades ago.  If all U.S.-China trade were to cease tomorrow, I guess China may perhaps endure a little recession, and the U.S. would just crash.

There must be some motive for damnfool policies that hurt the U.S. more than the CCP.  I’ll file that under “just asking questions”.

Since you’re so opposed to the CCP, I must ask, what have you done against them lately?  Let me guess…  Have you contributed code or money to the Tor Project, which plays a perpetual cat-and-mouse game to help Chinese citizens illegally evade Great Firewall (GFW) censorship to reach the free Internet?  Do you support a liberal asylum policy for active Chinese dissidents who need to flee their country?  Did you oppose DOGE’s cuts to Radio Free Asia, which is basically American information warfare against the CCP (and the DPRK)?  Do you…?

Given that you’re so very strongly opposed to the CCP that you’ll embrace trashing the U.S. economy to hurt them less than this hurts us, it’s fair to ask.

(Not even asking if you constructively supported the WHO’s friendly diplomatic attempt to elicit cooperation from the Chinese government in the WHO investigation of the origins of SARS-CoV-2.  That wasn’t against the CCP.  It was politely asking the Chinese government please to work with the politically neutral WHO on a scientific issue that literally affects all humans.  It’s not a request that U.S. Republicans would understand.)

I feel that pretending that this is incompetence is also playing into the agenda. It’s all intentional, and obviously so. They add laws and remove consistent enforcement so that they can then profit off gatekeeping the justice, or off of helping their friends bypass the same laws. The “art” of the “deal”.

There’s also a lot of incompetence mixed in.  The problem arises (in my mind at least) when people forget about the agenda.
